sentences.text: This creature had wings equipped with claws and a lengthy bony tail.
Fossil traces reveal downy feathers covering its tail, chest, and neck.
The lack of large feathers indicates it could not fly.
Scientists first named this species Aurornis xui in 2013.
The specific name honors the paleontologist Xu Xing.
A 2013 phylogenetic analysis placed it within the avian lineage, in a position more basal than Archaeopteryx.
It is classified within the unranked family Avialae.
Aurornis belongs to the family Anchiornithidae.
A 2017 re-evaluation of the Harlem Archaeopteryx specimen found Aurornis to be an anchiornithid.
Analysis places its origin in the Tiaojishan Formation, dating to the late Jurassic Oxfordian stage about 160 million years ago.
Remains were discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation of Liaoning, China.
It lived during the Bathonian to Kimmeridgian stages, between 168.2 and 152.21 million years ago.
A 2014 analysis by Brusatte et al. recovered Aurornis outside Avialae, classifying it as a troodontid closely related to Anchiornis.
The classification of A. xui as a bird is controversial because there are multiple different definitions of the word "bird".
Paleontologist Luis Chiappe argued that the forelimb of A. xui is too short to be that of a true bird.
A 2017 study suggested that Aurornis might be a junior synonym of Anchiornis because its traits fall within Anchiornis's range of variation.
